# Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#sports-agent)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-27**

[Original source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.33700v1) · arXiv:2611.33700v1, 25 November 2026, 48 pages.

**Reading coverage:** Read the 48-page paper through Sections 1–9 and Appendices A–B, including Algorithm 1, 17 figures, 11 tables and the two worked policy/skill changes. The public evaluation protocols in Appendix A were checked against Table 3.

## Research question

A conversational analytics agent may fill in facts the available sources do not establish, or return a correct statistic for only part of the period or population a user requested.

## Method

The feedback engine assesses answers and traces, identifies failures and proposes scoped changes to prompts or skills for replay and evaluation. Model training uses generated questions, filtered trajectories, supervised fine-tuning and a subsequent RL stage. The paper distinguishes verifiable SQL stages from open analytical tasks scored by judges.

## Evaluation

The paper reports sports-domain evaluations and separate runs of LiveSQLBench and BIRD-Interact. In the public BIRD-Interact experiments, an agent spends a limited interaction budget, queries the database, and may clarify with a simulated user. The two subtasks determine the normalized reward. Each public benchmark task was run once.

## What the results support

A prompt edit combining mandatory factual retrieval, evidence grounding and disclosure of missing information raised the held-out composite score from 65.31 to 71.10. In a separate experiment, the post-RL model scored 54.0% on BIRD-Interact Lite and 41.0% on Full under the authors’ simulator configuration.

## Limits and qualifications

The prompt edit changes multiple behaviors at once. The composite score cannot attribute the gain to expressing uncertainty. BIRD-Interact rewards task completion and partial progress, without separately scoring question quality or identifying intrinsically unanswerable requests. The product evaluation uses a model judge for factual correctness and response length as a proxy for richness.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Documents two responses to an incomplete answer: seek additional data when the request can be resolved, or report the supported portion and identify the missing evidence. The study gives examples and aggregate scores rather than a separate test of when to choose each response.

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

The experiment does not measure outcomes with human users or give a separate score for resolving ambiguity. |
| Is the product’s overall quality gain independently verified factual accuracy? | The 500-question comparison uses an LLM judge for factual correctness and average response length for richness. The baseline and evolved systems differ in both their model and their surrounding tools and instructions. | Section 6.2 and Figure 13 | Interpret these as author-reported product-level measurements under the stated metrics; they do not identify the contribution of the uncertainty policy. |
| Can a better-grounded answer still omit part of the requested statistic? | In a separate skill revision, the original trajectory retrieved regular-season data alone for an overall career-statistics question. The revised query included playoff data and reported both categories. This comparison started with the evidence-grounding prompt already in place. | Section 4.5.2 and Figure 9, pp. 21–24 | The replay illustrates a coverage problem that the global grounding instruction did not fix. The two case studies used different held-out comparisons; their gains cannot be added. |
